title: Comparing Strings with ==
summary: Why == can say two equal words are different, and how equals compares what Strings actually say.
objectives: Explain the difference between two Strings having the same text and being the same object.
Predict when `==` gives false for two Strings that look identical.
Write comparisons that do not crash when a String is null.

blocks.text: A program asks a question and checks the answer. The student typed yes, the program compared it with `"yes"`, and still said it did not recognise it. The comparison used `==`.

bad.title: Compares objects

good.title: Compares text

blocks.note: `new String("yes")` stands in for text that arrives while the program runs, such as input from a Scanner. Both versions hold the same three letters; only `equals` looks at the letters.

blocks.text: A String variable does not hold the text itself. It holds a reference: directions to a String object somewhere in memory. For objects, `==` asks whether two references point to the same object. `equals` asks whether the two objects contain the same characters.

blocks.caption: typed and the literal "yes" after String typed = new String("yes");
blocks.note: Two objects with the same text. `==` compares the arrows, so it says false. `equals` compares the text, so it says true.

blocks.caption: Two ways of asking "is it the same?"
rows: the characters, with YES the same as yes

sections.title: Why it sometimes seems to work

blocks.text: What makes this mistake dangerous is that `==` often gives the right answer while you test. Java keeps one shared copy of each string literal written in your code, so two variables set from the same literal point to the same object. Text that is built or read while the program runs is a new object.

blocks.caption: Reading the three lines
rows: no, c is a new object

blocks.title: Tests that pass for the wrong reason
blocks.text: If you only test with literals typed into your code, `==` passes. The same program fails as soon as the text comes from a user, a file or a calculation. Use `equals` every time you mean the same text.

blocks.caption: Which comparison to use

blocks.title: Put the literal first
blocks.text: `"yes".equals(typed)` gives false when `typed` is null. `typed.equals("yes")` crashes with a `NullPointerException`, because there is no object to call equals on. Starting with the literal is a habit that removes a whole class of crashes.

blocks.note: `!=` is just `==` turned around, so it has the same problem: every line read is a new object, so the loop never ends.
A single letter is still a String when it is in double quotes. A `char` in single quotes, `'A'`, is a primitive and `==` is right for it.

blocks.question: Why can a == b be true when a and b were both set to "yes" in the code?
options: Java shares one object for identical literals
Because yes is a short word
blocks.explanation: Identical string literals share a single object, so both variables point to it. Text made while the program runs does not.

items: `==` on Strings asks whether they are the same object, not whether they say the same thing.
Use `equals` to compare text, and `equalsIgnoreCase` when case should not matter.
`==` may pass with literals and then fail with real input, so tests can hide this bug.
Write `"literal".equals(variable)` to stay safe when the variable might be null.
